outcome.decaying: ORBIT UNSTABLE — PERIAPSIS INSIDE THE ATMOSPHERE
setup.argPeri.info: Which way the closest point of the orbit faces. On a circle it does nothing; on an ellipse it turns the whole ellipse about the parent.
setup.bodyDiameter.info:
The diameter of the rocket's body. The reference area A = πd²/4 follows from it, and drag is applied to that.

The relationship is quadratic: a rocket twice as wide catches four times the air. Shape is not modelled — everything that does not reduce to area is hidden in the drag coefficient.
setup.cd.info:
The drag coefficient. Drag is computed as ½·ρ·v²·Cd·A, so the relationship is linear.

The model knows nothing about the rocket's shape and does not vary Cd with Mach number: this is one averaged figure for the whole flight. For a slender launcher 0.3–0.5 is reasonable, though real vehicles climb well above that briefly around Mach 1.
setup.composition.info:
The mole fractions of the gases in the atmosphere. They are normalised automatically, so percentages or any other proportions will do.

Exactly two things come out of the mixture: the molar mass — a heavy gas hugs the surface and gives a small scale height — and the adiabatic index γ, which fixes the speed of sound. Nothing else depends on it: there is no chemistry in the model.
setup.cutoff.info:
How many seconds after ignition to shut the engine down rather than run the tanks dry. Zero means burn to the last drop.

This is the main instrument of a precise insertion: the orbit you end up in is decided by when the last stage stops. A few extra seconds of thrust raise the apoapsis by hundreds of kilometres.
setup.density.info:
The planet's mean density. The mass follows from it and the radius: M = ρ·(4/3)πR³.

Handy when you would rather say what the body is made of than pick a number: a rocky planet sits near 5500 kg/m³, an icy or gassy one at a third of that. Earth is 5514.
setup.diameter.info:
The planet's diameter. Together with the second independent figure — mass, density or surface gravity — it fixes everything else: the gravitational parameter μ = GM, the surface acceleration and the orbital speeds.

A large radius at the same density means both stronger gravity and a faster orbit: circular speed grows roughly as √(R·g). A small planet forgives almost any rocket; a large one forgives almost none.
setup.dryMass.info:
The mass of the stage without propellant: tanks, engines, structure. It has to be accelerated just like the payload, but it adds no propellant.

This is what limits a stage's Δv. Tsiolkovsky cares about the ratio of start mass to end mass, and the dry mass is the denominator you cannot get below.
setup.ecc.info:
How far from circular the orbit is. Zero is a circle; 0.9 is a long thin ellipse that spends most of its time far out and crosses the near part quickly.

The sphere of influence is computed from the semi-major axis alone, so a very eccentric moon will reach outside its own sphere near apoapsis. Nothing breaks, but the capture geometry stops making sense.
setup.ignitionDelay.info:
The pause between separation and lighting this stage, when the mode is set to a delay.

A short pause simply loses a little speed to gravity. A long one turns into a ballistic coast towards apoapsis — though the "at apoapsis" mode is easier for that, since it finds the moment itself.
setup.ispSL.info:
Specific impulse at the planet's surface pressure. Between this and the vacuum figure, Isp is interpolated linearly against ambient pressure.

This is where the thrust loss at liftoff comes from. An engine built for vacuum shows a wide gap; with no atmosphere the figure simply never matters.
setup.ispVac.info:
Specific impulse in vacuum, in seconds. It is really the exhaust velocity divided by g₀: 300 s means 2943 m/s.

The defining number of an engine. It alone fixes a stage's Δv for a given mass ratio, and together with thrust it sets the propellant flow. Kerosene and oxygen give around 310–350 s, hydrogen upwards of 450.
setup.mass.info:
The planet's mass. With the radius it gives the gravitational parameter μ = GM, which is all gravity knows about a planet. Surface acceleration, circular speed and escape speed all follow from it.

The density and gravity below are derived and update as you type. To define the planet through one of those instead, use the radio buttons above.
setup.meanAnom.info:
Where the body is at liftoff, measured along its orbit. This is the launch window: whether a transfer arrives at the moon or at the empty space it left is decided here.

Nothing in this simulator is tied to a date, so the shipped figures put the bodies where they make a picture worth looking at rather than where they were on any particular morning.
setup.orbitAltitude.info:
The altitude you are aiming for. It steers nothing: the rocket is flown by the pitch programme alone.

It drives the dashed ring on the flight screen, the circular speed shown below, and the estimate of what is needed for orbit at the bottom. A target, not an autopilot.
setup.payload.info:
Payload is the mass of whatever the launch exists for: a satellite, a spacecraft, cargo. It rides all the way to orbit and is never dropped, so it counts towards the mass during every phase of the flight and in every stage of the rocket equation.

Adding to it costs more than it looks: lifting one more tonne needs propellant to accelerate that tonne, and then more propellant to accelerate that propellant. The Δv margin at the bottom of the screen falls noticeably faster than the mass rises.
setup.pitchHintAngles: 90° is straight up, 0° is the horizon.
setup.propellant.info:
The stage's working mass — fuel and oxidiser together. It is consumed at a constant rate while the engine runs.

The burn time is that mass divided by the flow, both shown below. Adding propellant pays off only up to a point: Δv grows logarithmically while the mass to lift grows linearly.
setup.readyHint: Ready to launch. Press Enter or the button on the right.
setup.rootNote: The root of the system: everything else goes round it.
setup.rotationPeriod.info:
How long the planet takes to turn once. The launch pad rides with it and hands the rocket 2πR/T for free — on Earth that is 465 m/s if you launch east from the equator.

The atmosphere turns with the planet too, so drag is computed against moving air rather than against the inertial frame. Zero means a planet that does not rotate.
setup.semiMajor.info:
The average distance from the parent body. It sets the orbital period on its own: T = 2π√(a³/μ), so a moon twice as far out takes 2.8 times as long to go round.

Gm is a million kilometres. The Moon sits at 0.384; the Earth at 149.6 from the Sun.
setup.sepDelay.info:
The pause between a stage shutting down and separating. For that whole time the spent stage is still attached and still has to be carried.

In reality the delay lets the thrust tail off and the mechanism clear. Here it is simply a few seconds of dead weight.
setup.stageLimit: Four stages is the limit here.
setup.surfaceGravity.info:
The gravitational acceleration at the surface. The mass follows from it and the radius: M = g·R²/G.

The most direct way to describe a planet: g says outright how hard it will be to leave the pad. The thrust-to-weight figure at the bottom of the screen is measured against it.
setup.surfacePressure.info:
The pressure at the surface. The whole barometric profile stands on it: the density at any altitude is proportional to it, and so is the drag.

It also sets the reference for specific impulse — the sea-level Isp applies at exactly this pressure, and Isp is interpolated linearly between it and vacuum. Zero means a planet with no atmosphere.
setup.temperature.info:
The temperature at the surface. It sets the scale height H = RT/(Mg): the warmer the gas, the more slowly it thins out with altitude.

It also fixes the speed of sound, and with it the Mach number and the whole transonic part of the climb. Higher up the temperature follows the lapse rates in the layer table.
setup.throttle.info:
The fraction of full thrust, 0 to 1. It stays constant for the whole burn.

The flow drops in proportion, so the propellant lasts longer while the total Δv is unchanged — only the rate of spending it. Throttling down keeps acceleration and dynamic pressure in check, at the price of a longer climb.
setup.thrustVac.info:
The engine's thrust in vacuum at full throttle. With the specific impulse it sets the mass flow: ṁ = F/(Isp·g₀).

At the surface the thrust is lower — ambient pressure pushes back on the nozzle exit. The model holds the flow constant and varies the thrust with altitude, following the specific impulse.
setup.timeLimit.info:
How much simulated time the flight is given. When it runs out the run stops with a time-limit verdict.

It exists for ballistic arcs that would otherwise take a very long time to come down, and for orbits where nothing further is going to happen.
setup.upperBoundary.info:
The altitude above which the model treats the air as absent. Density there is exactly zero, and so is drag.

It is also the success threshold: an orbit counts as achieved once the periapsis clears this mark. Put it where the density is already negligible, or a flight will be declared a success while the rocket is still in the air.
setup.warnDv: Total Δv falls short even before losses.
setup.warnTwr: Thrust-to-weight below 1 — the vehicle will not leave the pad.
